title: Sudoku Solver & Constraint Satisfaction
summary: Solving Sudoku as a constraint-satisfaction backtracking search, and the ordering heuristics — like minimum-remaining-values — that keep it fast in practice.

slides.markdown:
Sudoku is [N-Queens](n-queens)'s more constrained cousin: instead of one rule (no shared row/column/diagonal), every empty cell must satisfy three simultaneous constraints — its digit can't repeat in its row, its column, or its 3×3 box. Framed generally, this is a **constraint satisfaction problem (CSP)**: a set of variables, each with a domain of legal values, and constraints between them that a full assignment must satisfy.

The backtracking engine is the same choose/explore/unexplore template used throughout this group — what's genuinely new here is that **which cell to fill next, and in what order to try its candidates, changes the search's real-world speed by orders of magnitude**, even though every valid ordering is equally correct.

Map Sudoku onto the CSP vocabulary directly: **variables** are the empty cells; each variable's **domain** is the digits 1–9 not yet ruled out; **constraints** are the row/column/box uniqueness rules linking variables to each other. "Solve the puzzle" becomes "find an assignment of a value to every variable that satisfies every constraint simultaneously."

This reframing matters because it's the same lens that applies to map coloring, cryptarithmetic puzzles, and scheduling problems — Sudoku isn't a one-off algorithm, it's one instance of a general CSP-solving pattern: backtracking search plus constraint propagation, which the rest of this topic builds out concretely.

slides.sectionTitle: Precomputing constraint sets for O(1) checks
slides.markdown:
Maintain nine row sets, nine column sets, and nine box sets of digits already placed. Checking whether `digit` is legal at `(row, col)` becomes three O(1) membership checks — `digit not in rows[row]`, `digit not in cols[col]`, `digit not in boxes[box_index(row, col)]` — instead of scanning up to 9+9+9 cells on every single trial digit at every single cell.

This is the identical trade seen in [N-Queens](n-queens): rescanning the board for conflicts is correct but wastefully repeats work already known from earlier placements, while maintained sets turn that same logical check into a constant-time lookup. Placing a digit adds it to all three relevant sets; undoing a placement removes it from all three.

slides.sectionTitle: Always picking the first empty cell
slides.markdown:
A working but slow default: scan the board top-left to bottom-right and fill the first empty cell found, every time. This is correct — every valid ordering of cells reaches the same solutions — but it can multiply the effective search space enormously, because a cell with 8 legal candidates left explored first will branch far more widely than one with only 1 or 2 legal candidates left.

The wasted work compounds: a wide early branch means every one of its many sub-branches gets explored before backtracking, most of which will eventually fail anyway once a more-constrained cell elsewhere on the board rules them out. Choosing *which* empty cell to fill next, not just filling in a fixed order, is the single biggest lever on real-world Sudoku-solver performance.

The **minimum-remaining-values (MRV) heuristic**: instead of the first empty cell, fill the empty cell with the **fewest legal digits remaining** first. A cell down to exactly one legal digit is effectively forced — filling it first commits to that near-certain choice immediately and lets its constraint ripple out to neighboring cells before any wide, uncertain branch gets explored.

The intuition: a highly constrained cell fails fast if it's actually going to fail (few or zero options to try), so choosing it first either makes rapid, low-branching progress or discovers a dead end quickly — both outcomes are better than burning search time on a wide-open cell whose real constraints only become clear after other cells nearby get filled in.

slides.sectionTitle: How placing a digit shrinks neighboring candidate sets
slides.markdown:
![Placing 5 in one cell highlights every other cell in its row, column, and box whose candidate list just lost the digit 5](assets/sudoku-constraint-propagation.svg)

Every cell sharing that row, column, or box just lost "5" as a legal candidate — which is exactly the information MRV needs to re-rank which cell to fill next. This is the mechanical link between placing one digit and the *next* cell selection: constraint propagation isn't a separate phase bolted on afterward, it's the direct consequence of maintaining accurate candidate sets after every placement.

assets.alt: Placing 5 in one cell highlights every other cell in its row, column, and box whose candidate list just lost the digit 5

slides.markdown:
| | Plain backtracking | Backtracking + constraint propagation |
|---|---|---|
| When candidates are eliminated | Only checked at the moment a digit is tried | Eliminated proactively the instant a neighboring cell is filled, before that cell is ever visited |
| Cell selection | Fixed order or simple heuristic | MRV using live-updated candidate counts |
| Typical speed on hard puzzles | Can be dramatically slower — explores many branches only to fail deep | Often orders of magnitude faster — many cells get down to one legal option before ever being explicitly searched |
| Extra bookkeeping | None | Candidate sets per cell must be kept in sync with every placement and every undo |

Plain backtracking with O(1) legality checks is already correct and reasonably fast for easy puzzles. Constraint propagation plus MRV is what separates a solver that struggles on genuinely hard, near-worst-case puzzles from one that solves them in a fraction of a second — the same gap seen between a naive board rescan and a maintained-set approach, one level more sophisticated.

slides.sectionTitle: Re-validating the whole board on every placement
slides.markdown:
A tempting but wasteful correctness check: after placing a digit, rescan the entire board to confirm no rule is violated anywhere. This is correct, but it's checking far more than what could possibly have changed — placing one digit at `(row, col)` can only ever create a new conflict within that specific row, that specific column, and that specific 3×3 box; every other row, column, and box is provably unaffected and doesn't need re-checking.

The fix is the same principle as O(1) legality checks generally: only re-validate the row, column, and box that the just-placed digit actually belongs to. Re-validating the whole board on every single placement turns an O(1) or O(9) check into an O(81) one, and that waste is paid on every trial digit at every cell throughout the entire search.

slides.sectionTitle: Generalizing the pattern to any CSP
slides.markdown:
The exact same shape — variables, domains, constraints, backtracking search, MRV-style ordering, and propagating eliminations after each assignment — solves **any** constraint satisfaction problem, not just Sudoku. Map coloring (variables are regions, domain is the color set, constraint is "adjacent regions differ") and cryptarithmetic (variables are letters, domain is 0–9, constraint is the arithmetic equation holding with no leading zero) fit the identical template with different variables, domains, and constraint-checking functions plugged in.

Recognizing an unfamiliar problem as "this is a CSP" is itself the valuable interview skill — once that framing clicks, the solving approach (backtracking search, most-constrained-variable-first, propagate eliminations after each placement) transfers directly, rather than needing to invent a new algorithm from scratch for every new constraint-shaped problem you encounter.
